scope: Named fig (Ficus carica) cultivars that gardeners grow in zone 6b/7a: in the ground with winter protection (most figs die back and regrow from the roots there), or in pots brought into a garage or cellar for winter. Cultivars sellers describe as cold hardy are tagged. Unnamed seedlings and the ornamental climbing fig (Ficus pumila) are left out. Prices are for one plant of the size noted (usually a 1-gallon pot).

varieties.name: Chicago Hardy
varieties.summary: The standard cold-climate fig: dies back in hard winters and still fruits on new growth.
varieties.description: Medium purple-brown figs with a strawberry-red interior. Widely grown in the Northeast and Midwest because it reliably regrows from the roots after a hard winter and bears on new wood the same summer. Sellers rate it to zone 6 in the ground, colder with winter protection.

varieties.name: Celeste
varieties.summary: Small, very sweet violet-brown 'sugar fig' with a closed eye.
varieties.description: A Southern heirloom producing small violet-brown figs with very sweet amber-pink flesh; the closed eye helps keep out insects and rain. Hardier than most figs once established and often grown in zone 6–7 with winter protection. Ripens mid-summer.

varieties.name: Brown Turkey
varieties.summary: Common, dependable brown fig that bears a breba and a main crop.
varieties.description: Medium to large copper-brown figs with pinkish amber flesh and a mild, sweet flavor. A vigorous, productive tree that regrows readily after winter dieback, which makes it a common choice for northern gardens with some protection. Fruit quality varies somewhat among the strains sold under this name.

varieties.name: Olympian
varieties.summary: Large purple-brown fig selected in the Pacific Northwest for cold tolerance.
varieties.description: Selected in Olympia, Washington, and grown for its cold tolerance and late leaf-out, which helps it avoid spring frost damage. Bears large purple-brown figs with sweet red-amber flesh. A good candidate for a sheltered spot in zone 6–7.

varieties.name: Marseilles
varieties.summary: Small to medium pale green-yellow fig with white, honey-sweet flesh.
varieties.description: An old white fig with pale green to yellowish skin and nearly white, very sweet flesh. Often grouped with Lattarula and other hardy white figs grown in cooler climates. Ripens mid-season.

varieties.name: Petite Negri
varieties.summary: Compact, early dark fig suited to pots and short seasons.
varieties.description: A naturally small, compact tree that fruits young, making it a favorite for containers that come indoors for winter. Bears small to medium dark purple figs with red flesh, usually with an early breba crop. Ripens early enough for northern summers.

varieties.name: LSU Purple
varieties.summary: Productive purple fig from Louisiana State University's fig program.
varieties.description: Medium dark purple figs with sweet, light strawberry flesh, often bearing more than one crop a year in long seasons. Valued for productivity and resistance to leaf disease. Needs a protected spot or container culture in zone 6b.

varieties.name: Violette de Bordeaux
varieties.summary: Small, intensely flavored near-black fig from France; compact tree.
varieties.description: A French heirloom with small blackish-purple figs and deep red, jammy, rich flesh. The tree stays compact, so it works well in a pot, and it fruits on new wood after dieback. Often counted among the best-flavored dark figs.

varieties.name: Green Ischia
varieties.summary: Green-skinned fig with strawberry-red flesh, from the island of Ischia.
varieties.description: Bears medium figs with green to yellow-green skin and bright strawberry-red, sweet flesh, so birds tend to leave them alone. Productive and moderately hardy; best with winter protection in zone 6b.

varieties.name: Conadria
varieties.summary: Light green fig with white to pink flesh, bred in California.
varieties.description: A California-bred fig with thin light green skin and white to pinkish, mildly sweet flesh, resistant to splitting and souring. A vigorous tree that fruits on new wood. Best in a sheltered spot or container in zone 6b.

varieties.name: O'Rourke
varieties.summary: Light brown fig with amber flesh from the Louisiana fig program.
varieties.description: Medium light brown to bronze figs with sweet amber flesh and a tight eye. An early-ripening, productive variety from Louisiana's fig breeding program. Needs protection or container culture in zone 6b.

varieties.name: Panache
varieties.summary: Striking green-and-yellow striped 'Tiger' fig with red flesh.
varieties.description: An ornamental and edible fig with green-and-yellow striped skin and deep red, berry-like flesh. Needs a long, warm season to ripen well, so it is best in a pot or a hot, protected spot in zone 6b.

varieties.name: Brunswick
varieties.summary: Large bronze-skinned fig with amber flesh; an old hardy variety.
varieties.description: An old variety, also sold as Magnolia, with large bronze to light brown figs and amber-pink flesh. Known for regrowing from the roots after cold winters. Good fresh and excellent for preserves.

varieties.name: Desert King
varieties.summary: Green fig that sets a big early breba crop without pollination.
varieties.description: Bears a large breba crop of green figs with strawberry-red flesh on last year's wood, ripening in early summer. Does well in cool-summer climates, but because its main crop is on old wood, winter dieback costs the year's crop in zone 6b unless the tree is protected.

varieties.name: Lattarula
varieties.summary: Italian white 'honey fig' with sweet amber flesh; cold tolerant.
varieties.description: An Italian heirloom with yellow-green skin and very sweet amber flesh, often sold as Italian Honey Fig. Reliable in cooler summers and regrows after winter dieback, which makes it a common choice for northern gardens.

varieties.name: Little Ruby
varieties.summary: Dwarf fig for containers with dark skin and ruby-red flesh.
varieties.description: A compact, slow-growing fig that suits pots that come indoors in winter. Bears medium figs with dark purple-brown skin and ruby-red, sweet flesh. A good choice where in-ground figs are marginal.

varieties.name: Dauphine
varieties.summary: French fig with a large breba crop of purple fruit.
varieties.description: A French variety with large purple-violet figs and sweet pink-red flesh, known for an especially large early breba crop. Main-crop figs follow later in summer in warm years.

varieties.name: Madeleine des Deux Saisons
varieties.summary: French white fig that bears in two seasons.
varieties.description: A French white fig whose name means 'Madeleine of the two seasons' for its breba and main crops. Bears pale green-yellow figs with sweet, honeyed flesh, and does well in cooler climates.

varieties.name: Sultane
varieties.summary: Dark purple French fig with deep red flesh.
varieties.description: A French variety bearing medium to large dark purple figs with deep red, rich flesh. Grown for its flavor and productivity in cooler summers.

varieties.name: Peter's Honey
varieties.summary: Bright yellow-green fig with very sweet amber flesh.
varieties.description: An Italian variety brought to Oregon, with glossy greenish-yellow skin and dark amber, very sweet flesh. Needs warmth to ripen well, so it is best in a sunny, sheltered spot or a pot in zone 6b.

varieties.name: Pastilliere
varieties.summary: Small, early dark fig from France; compact and productive.
varieties.description: A French fig bearing small dark purple figs with red flesh, ripening early. Compact and productive, which suits containers and short seasons.

varieties.name: Nordland
varieties.summary: Cold-tolerant fig said to survive about 10°F.
varieties.description: Sold by Raintree as a cold-tolerant selection said to survive temperatures near 10°F. Bears purple-brown figs with sweet flesh on a tree that suits cool northern summers.

varieties.name: Fignomenal
varieties.summary: Very dwarf patio fig that stays under 3 feet; made for pots.
varieties.description: A patented dwarf fig that stays small enough for a pot on a patio or windowsill. Bears medium brown-purple figs over a long season. Overwinters indoors or in a garage in zone 6b.

varieties.name: Brooklyn Dark
varieties.summary: East Coast selection with brown-black skin and red, melon-honey flavored flesh.
varieties.description: An East Coast selection from Trees of Joy Nursery. Brown-to-black figs with red flesh and a rich melon-honey flavor, with a breba crop in July–August and a main crop in October. Self-fruitful; the seller rates it to about 0–5°F and says it is valued in the Northeast.

varieties.name: Black Bethlehem
varieties.summary: Purple-black fig from Bethlehem, PA with an intense strawberry flavor.
varieties.description: Discovered growing in Bethlehem, PA and re-discovered on the East Coast. Purple-black skin, red flesh and strawberry-like flavor, ripening August through October. One Green World describes it as similar to Chicago Hardy in flavor, production and cold tolerance, and self-fertile.

varieties.name: Gene's Vashon
varieties.summary: Puget Sound fig with green skin ripening purple and sweet amber-red flesh.
varieties.description: Grown on cool Vashon Island in Puget Sound, where it ripens breba figs reliably; the seller notes it may be a renamed Brown Turkey variant. Sweet fruit with green-to-purple skin and amber-to-red flesh, long-necked, main crop from September. Self-fertile and rated hardy to at least 0°F.

varieties.name: Hunt
varieties.summary: Old Georgia fig with violet-brown skin and light red flesh.
varieties.description: Bred in Georgia in the 1920s. Violet-brown skin with light red flesh. One Green World rates it to USDA zone 6 and calls it one of the most cold-hardy figs for Southeastern growers.

varieties.name: Gabe's Gold
varieties.summary: Yellow-skinned, berry-sweet fig found wild in Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains.
varieties.description: Selected from a wild fig found in a drainage in the San Gabriel Mountains north of Azusa, California. Small, very sweet figs have yellow skin and light red flesh with a light berry flavor. Self-fruitful tree that bears 1–2 years after planting and ripens in September–October; rated to about 0–5°F (zone 7b) by One Green World.

varieties.name: Blanche d'Argenteuil
varieties.summary: French fig with a breba and main crop of sweet, floral yellow-green fruit.
varieties.description: A fig from the suburbs of Paris, France. Fruit has yellow-green skin and amber-to-red flesh with a sweet, delicate floral flavor. Bears a breba crop and a main crop from July through October and handles rain well; rated to about 0–5°F (zone 7b) by One Green World.

varieties.name: Atreano
varieties.summary: Light green-skinned fig with dark amber flesh that ripens in late summer.
varieties.description: Fruit has light green skin and dark amber flesh with a sweet, flavorful taste. Ripens from late July to early August with a yield of 10–15 lbs or more per plant. One Green World rates it to about 0–5°F (zone 7); origin not stated.

varieties.name: Jack Lily
varieties.summary: LSU-bred honey-type fig that resists splitting in wet autumns.
varieties.description: An early-to-mid-season honey fig from Louisiana State University's fig breeding program. Yellow-skinned fruit has amber-red to pink flesh with a strawberry-jam sweetness and resists splitting in wet weather. Self-fertile, ripening late August through October; rated to about 0–5°F (zone 7b) by One Green World.

breeder.name: Louisiana State University fig breeding program

varieties.name: Black Spanish
varieties.summary: Naturally dwarf, dark mahogany fig suited to containers.
varieties.description: Grown for many years in Oregon. Dark mahogany skin with pink, strawberry-flavored flesh; very sweet, juicy and firm, good fresh, preserved or dried. A naturally dwarf tree (8–10 ft) that suits container culture and can bear two crops a year, ripening late July to early August; rated to zone 7 by One Green World.

varieties.name: Domenico Tauro
varieties.summary: Italian fig with a large early breba crop, suited to short seasons.
varieties.description: An Italian variety with large, sweet figs that have purplish-brown skin and blush-pink flesh. Produces a large early breba crop and is described as suited to short-season growers. Rated to about 0–5°F (zone 7) by One Green World.

varieties.name: GE Neri
varieties.summary: Rare Italian fig with dark skin and sweet, jammy red flesh.
varieties.description: Described by Perfect Plants Nursery as a rare Italian cultivar with dark skin and sweet, reddish, berry-tinged flesh in roughly tennis-ball-sized figs. Self-pollinating and suited to containers, reaching about 6-10 ft tall. The seller rates it for USDA zones 7-9, so zone 6b needs winter protection or an indoor overwintered pot.

varieties.name: LSU Gold
varieties.summary: Yellow-gold fig from Louisiana State University with honey-sweet flesh.
varieties.description: Medium to large figs with yellow-gold skin and amber flesh, tasting sweet and honey-like with berry notes. Vigorous, self-pollinating plant of about 8-10 ft that does well in containers and gives an early-summer and a late-summer-to-fall crop. Rated for zones 7-10 in the ground; colder areas grow it in pots brought indoors for winter.

breeder.name: Louisiana State University fig breeding program

varieties.name: Black Mission
varieties.summary: Classic dark purple-black fig with strawberry-colored, jammy flesh.
varieties.description: Pear-shaped figs with dark purple-black skin and strawberry-colored flesh that turns rich and jammy when ripe; Perfect Plants says it originates in Spain. Main harvest runs late summer to early fall, with a possible small early crop in warm areas. The seller rates it for zones 7-10 with limited cold hardiness, so it suits a pot overwintered indoors at zone 6b.

varieties.name: Champagne
varieties.summary: Yellow LSU fig with gold-to-caramel flesh and better leaf-disease resistance than Celeste.
varieties.description: Developed by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station and released by the LSU AgCenter in 2007, after being known informally as 'Golden Celeste'. Yellow-skinned figs, somewhat larger than Celeste, have gold-to-caramel flesh and ripen at about the same time as Celeste, in early July in Baton Rouge. It is a common fig that needs no pollination, is slightly more resistant than Celeste to defoliation from fig rust and leaf spot, and the eye is only partly closed; LSU notes good cold resistance.
varieties.one_liner: The yellow Celeste-type that holds its leaves better

breeder.name: LSU AgCenter (Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station) fig breeding program

varieties.name: LSU Tiger
varieties.summary: LSU fig with stripes on ripening fruit, on a smaller tree than Celeste.
varieties.description: Released by the LSU AgCenter in 2007 and named for the stripes that show on the fruit as it ripens. Figs are 30 to 50 percent larger than Celeste, borne on a relatively small tree, about half the size of a mature Celeste, with a long fruiting period. LSU sources disagree on timing, one saying it ripens about a week after Celeste and another a week earlier; the eye is not as tightly closed as Celeste's.
varieties.one_liner: The striped LSU fig on a compact, smaller tree

breeder.name: LSU AgCenter (Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station) fig breeding program

notes: Not the same as Panache, which is also sold as 'Tiger'.

varieties.name: Alma
varieties.summary: Late-season golden-brown Texas fig with rich, sweet amber flesh.
varieties.description: Bred by Texas A&M and released in 1975. Small to medium, pear-shaped golden-brown figs with amber flesh and a closed eye have a very sweet, rich flavor, though the skin is unattractive, and Alabama Extension rates them highly resistant to fruit rots. A late-ripening, very productive tree that bears young; Texas A&M calls it very frost-sensitive, especially when young, and best within about 200 miles of the Gulf, so at zone 6b it is a pot fig.
varieties.one_liner: The late, rot-resistant Texas fig with very sweet flesh

varieties.name: Kadota
varieties.summary: Classic greenish-white all-purpose fig with amber flesh.
varieties.description: A long-grown commercial California fig of the common type, also known as Dottato. Small to medium greenish-white to greenish-yellow figs with amber flesh and a medium eye are rich, sweet and used fresh, dried and canned; the breba crop is light to good and the main crop abundant. Vigorous, best in the Southwest and drier parts of the South, and rated fairly hardy by Alabama Extension.
varieties.one_liner: The classic green all-purpose fig for drying and canning

varieties.name: Sal's
varieties.summary: Small black fig from Long Island, said to be hardier than Celeste.
varieties.description: A small to medium black fig of unknown origin, introduced by a local nursery on Long Island. Alabama Extension calls it well adapted to the Northeast and extremely hardy, seemingly somewhat hardier than Celeste, with good flavor. Plants are vigorous and productive.
varieties.one_liner: The very cold-hardy black fig from Long Island

varieties.name: Osborn Prolific
varieties.summary: Very productive bronze fig with sweet, rich amber flesh.
varieties.description: Medium-sized bronze to brown figs with amber to light strawberry flesh and a sweet, rich flavor. Alabama Extension calls it hardy, very productive and well adapted in all fig-growing areas.
varieties.one_liner: The very productive bronze fig that does well almost anywhere

varieties.name: Excel
varieties.summary: Condit-bred yellow fig with amber flesh and superb flavor.
varieties.description: Bred by Ira Condit and released in 1975, and sometimes called Kadota Hybrid. Medium yellow figs, round to slightly flattened, have amber flesh with superb flavor. Well adapted in California; Alabama Extension says it seems very hardy.
varieties.one_liner: The yellow California hybrid with superb flavor

varieties.name: Tena
varieties.summary: Very sweet greenish-yellow Condit fig with light strawberry flesh.
varieties.description: Bred by Ira Condit and released in 1975. Medium to large greenish-yellow figs with light strawberry flesh are very sweet but not rich, and are grouped with the Adriatic-type drying figs in California. Widely adapted but prefers hot, dry weather; somewhat hardy.
varieties.one_liner: The very sweet green fig for hot, dry summers

varieties.name: Flanders
varieties.summary: Violet-striped greenish-yellow Condit fig with amber flesh.
varieties.description: Bred and released by Ira Condit in 1975. Medium greenish-yellow, pear-shaped figs with a long slender neck carry violet stripes and have amber flesh with fine flavor. Plants are vigorous but not particularly hardy, doing best on the West Coast.
varieties.one_liner: The violet-striped green fig with fine flavor

varieties.name: Sierra
varieties.summary: University of California fig with amber flesh and a very tight eye.
varieties.description: Released by the University of California in 2005. Yellow-green figs with amber flesh and a very tight eye have very good flavor; the breba crop is light, while the main crop is abundant and holds medium-to-large size well into fall. A common fig that needs no pollination.
varieties.one_liner: The UC fig whose main crop keeps its size into fall

varieties.name: Beall
varieties.summary: Purplish-black California seedling fig with amber flesh.
varieties.description: Found as a chance seedling in California in the 1920s. Medium to large purplish-black figs with amber flesh have very good flavor, with necked brebas and an oblate to pear-shaped main crop. Alabama Extension says it is well adapted in California and hardy in the South.
varieties.one_liner: The black California seedling with very good flavor

varieties.name: Adriatic
varieties.summary: Green drying fig with light strawberry flesh.
varieties.description: Medium-sized green to greenish-yellow, top-shaped figs with light strawberry flesh and good flavor; one of the Adriatic-type figs California uses for drying and fig paste. Alabama Extension rates it fairly hardy but notes it is very subject to mosaic virus.
varieties.one_liner: The green drying fig with strawberry flesh

varieties.name: Nero
varieties.summary: Large purplish-black fig with pink flesh and rich flavor.
varieties.description: Large purplish-black figs, flattened at the tip, have light pink flesh and very good to excellent, fairly sweet and rich flavor; the eye is medium and open. Alabama Extension calls it well adapted in the Southwest and South.
varieties.one_liner: The large black fig with rich pink flesh

varieties.name: Mary Lane
varieties.summary: Juicy yellow fig described as seedless.
varieties.description: A medium yellow fig of unknown identity said to have originated in California. Round, slightly flattened figs are very juicy and sweet and are described as seedless, so few seeds. Alabama Extension says it is well adapted in all fig areas.
varieties.one_liner: The juicy yellow fig with few seeds

varieties.name: Early Violet
varieties.summary: Very small chocolate-brown fig with an early main crop.
varieties.description: Small to very small chocolate-brown figs with amber to pink flesh and fair to good quality. It sets no breba crop, but the main crop is early-ripening. Alabama Extension notes it is susceptible to mosaic virus.
varieties.one_liner: The tiny early fig for a head start on the main crop
